title: Manunggul Jar
creator: Ancient Palawan Potters
description: In the Tabon Caves of Palawan, the Manunggul Jar is an exceptionally well-known secondary burial jar. The Manunggul Jar is dated to the late Neolithic Period and features an extremely detailed lid that has two human figurines in a boat as they represent a person's journey to the afterlife. The soul's journey to the afterlife represents a person's beliefs regarding spirituality, burial customs, and the skill of early Filipinos as artists, which confirms the importance of the Manunggul Jar as one of the most significant archeological finds in the Philippines.
subject: Burial Practices; Ancient Pottery; Neolithic Philippines; Spiritual Beliefs; Archaeology

title: Laguna Copperplate Inscription
creator: Unknown Ancient Filipino Scribe
description: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription is thought to be the oldest known written record found in the Philippines, dating back to 900 CE. The Laguna Copperplate Inscription has been inscribed onto a flat piece of thin copper and discusses the means by which debts were forgiven in the early political setup as a result of the early organized societies that existed at this time. The Laguna Copperplate Inscription also contains evidence of literacy, trade and cultural links to our neighboring Asian countries. The Laguna Copperplate Inscription serves to establish that organized societies existed long before Spain established itself in the Philippines by showing that pre-hispanic Filipinos had created systems for communication that were quite complex.
subject: Ancient Writing Systems; Philippine History; Pre-colonial Society; Trade; Archaeology

title: Butuan Ivory Seal
creator: Butuan Craftsmen
description: The Butuan Ivory Seal, a small carving made of ivory found on the excavation site in Butuan, Agusan del Norte, is thought to be an early method of marking documents or goods during trade. This artifact demonstrates the strong involvement of the early Filipinos in trade throughout all of Southwest Asia and the outstanding capabilities for artistry and commerce among those living in the Butuan area.

title: Balangay Boats
creator: Ancient Austronesian Boat Builders
description: Balangay Boats are old wood vessels found at Butuan that are recognized as using today's definitions as the earliest examples of marine vessels in the Philippines. These vessels were utilized by the early Filipinos of Austronesian descent as modes of transportatiom or trade to other islands and countries surrounding the Philippines. Each balangay boat was built entirely from nailed-together wooden planks — an engineering marvel — representing the long history of seafaring skills possessed by the early Filipino inhabitants of this region of the world.

title: Golden Tara
creator: Ancient Agusan Goldsmiths
description: The Golden Tara is an ancient gold statue that was found in Agusan; it is thought to depict a Hindu-Buddhist deity from the period before the Spanish had colonized the Philippines. This artifact is made from high-purity gold, which is a testament to the cultural and religious influences of early trade between India and Southeast Asian societies. The design of this statue exhibits the skillful craftsmanship of goldsmiths in the Philippines long ago and offers evidence of the thriving spiritual and artistic heritages that existed prior to colonization.

title: Surigao Treasure
creator: Pre-colonial Filipino Goldsmiths
description: The Surigao Treasure consists of many ancient gold ornaments, jewelry items, belts and ceremony objects, which were all found in Surigao del Sur. These artifacts emanate from before the period of Spanish colonization and illustrate the affluence, skill of workmanship, and social standing of early Filipino communities. The sophistication of their ornamentation and the use of pure gold demonstrate that the ancient Filipinos possessed a high degree of sophistication in their goldworking techniques and were well connected to other regional trading networks and networks of cultural exchange within Southeast Asia.
subject: Gold Jewelry; Wealth and Status; Ancient Filipino Craftsmanship; Trade; Archaeology

title: Calatagan Pot
creator: Ancient Tagalog Potters
description: The Calatagan Pot, a clay burial jar found in Batangas. It has important inscriptions engraved on its exterior surface. The pot may be associated with pre-colonial Philippine burial practices and ancient Filipino writing systems. This represents the spiritual beliefs, languages and everyday life of the Tagalog people in the early Philippines during the time prior to colonialism.
subject: Burial Traditions; Ancient Scripts; Pottery; Pre-colonial Culture; Archaeology

title: Angono Petroglyphs
creator: Prehistoric Austronesian hunter-gatherers
description: The Angono Petroglyphs are the Philippines' oldest known rock carvings, dating back to the late Neolithic period. More than a hundred stylized human and animal figures have been carved into a rock face at this site, believed to represent early forms of communication, ritual practices, or symbols used for healing by prehistoric communities. This site provides invaluable evidence of the art and culture, spiritual belief system, and everyday life of early Filipinos, prior to the written record in the Philippines.

title: Kamhantik Limestone Tombs
creator: Ancient pre-colonial Filipino
description: The Kamhantik Limestone Tombs, in Mulanay, Quezon Province, are an archaeological site of great significance that includes limestone coffins (burials) cut directly from large blocks of stone, skeletal remains and accompanying burial artifacts. Based on the tombs, archaeologists believe this site represents a well-organized, pre-colonial society that possessed an advanced knowledge of stone carving techniques and burial practices. The presence of these tombs suggests that a successful social structure existed, further defining the complexity and diversity of culture among the ancient communities of southern Luzon.

title: Banton Cloth
creator: Early Visayan weavers
description: Banton Cloth, which is one of the earliest existing cloth pieces from the Southeast Asian region, was found within a wooden coffin located in the area known as Banton Island in the Philippines. This cloth is comprised of a number of different types of fiber and is decorated with intricate geometric designs that were made using techniques for dyeing and weaving that resulted in highly skilled workmanship by the early Filipinos and reveal their impressive artistry prior to the arrival of European colonial authorities. Additionally, the Banton Cloth is indicative of the early trade patterns among various cultural groups, provides evidence of how people identified themselves through different methods and ways, and demonstrates how textile-making traditions are an influence on the way in which the culture of weaving in the Philippines has developed over time.

title: Maranao Okir Wood Carvings
creator: Maranao artisans
description: Maranao Okir utilize form and creative expression to create unique decorative art pieces created by the people of the Maranao tribe, who live in the Lanao del Sur region of Mindanao. Maranao culture has a rich tradition of creating Okir, which has flowing designs made with intricate line work that often utilize geometric figures (shapes) with influences from both the natural world (flora and fauna) and mythical creatures. Okir is also applied to various pieces of furniture (houses), special event-related items (boats), musical instruments, and ceremonial artifacts. Okir has both indigenous and Muslim cultural roots, and represents the identity through one's creation of Okir, as well as demonstrates the social status, pride, and prestige of the individuals associated with the Maranao tribes.

title: Ifugao Bulul
creator: Ifugao ritual carvers and spiritual artisans
description: The Ifugao Bulul is a carved wooden statue representing the spirit guardians of rice, and the ancestors of the people of Ifugao in the Cordillera region of the Philippines. These statues were traditionally placed in granaries and fields, and were believed to protect rice crops, foster fertility, and provide an abundance of rice at harvest time. Each Bulul was ritually ceremonially blessed, signifying the deep spiritual connections among agriculture, ancestors, and daily life in Ifugao culture. The Bulul still represents powerful symbols of Indigenous belief systems in the Philippines today.

title: T’boli T’nalak
creator: T’boli women weavers
description: The sacred textile, T’nalak, is made by the T’boli people of South Cotabato, using traditional handweaving techniques. Skilled women (known as “dreamweavers”) create these textiles, believing that the spirit guardian Fu Dalu reveals their designs in dreams. Creating T’nalak is very detail-oriented and requires a lot of patience, as the weavers use abaca fibers dyed in the traditional manner. T’nalak is used to create cultural items for rituals and ceremonies that represent identity and spirituality.

title: Kulintang Ensemble
creator: Maranao, Maguindanao, and Tausug musicians
description: The Kulintang Ensemble consists of a number of horizontally aligned gongs, with varying-gongs used to provide rhythm; in addition, drums are played along with these in order to add additional sound/texture while performing as part of their celebration, ritual, wedding, etc. culturally, this type of music is very spiritual(in addition to being social) and continues to remain a key component of filipino indigenous music.

title: Spoliarium
creator: Juan Luna
description: The Spoliarium is a large-scale oil painting by Juan Luna created in 1884 while living in Rome. This particular work depicts the remains of gladiators that had recently died being pulled off of the arena floor, underscoring how brutal and incredibly oppressive oppression really is. While the painting has historical significance, it is also commonly viewed as a visual representation of the struggles faced by Filipinos during the Spanish Colonial Period. As such, it is considered by many people to be one of the top masterpieces of Philippine Art and a powerful symbol of the national identity/resistance.
subject: Painting; Fine Arts; Spanish Colonial Philippines; History; National Identity

title: Bolinao Skull
creator: Pre-colonial Filipinos of Pangasinan
description: The Bolinao Skull of Pangasinan is a significant archaeological object because it represents some of the earliest documented ways in which the ancient Filipino peoples practised funerary customs. A notable feature of this skull is that gold had been affixed to the teeth of the deceased in the form of thin gold leaves, indicating that gold was not only a symbol of wealth but was also likely to have some form of ceremonial or ritualistic significance to the pre-colonial population. This skull is believed to have belonged to an individual of high rank, thus enhancing the evidence for social stratification of the early peoples of the Philippines. Additionally, the elaborate nature of this adornment provides further demonstration of the exceptional craftsmanship that existed in the goldsmithing processes developed by indigenous goldsmiths long before the arrival of the Spanish colonizers.

title: Maitum Anthropomorphic Jars
creator: Early Iron Age Filipinos (Sarangani/Maitum communities)
description: Discovered within Ayub Cave in Sarangani, the Maitum Anthropomorphic Jars have been regarded as one of the most extraordinary archaeological discoveries to be made in Southeast Asia. These jars are distinguished from other types of burial jars in that the jars are both physically shaped and decorated with features that are generally associated with human faces. These jars were used to hold human remains and funerary offerings during the Neolithic period and were used as burial vessels. The jars contain design attributes that illustrate that early Filipinos were capable of developing a sophisticated belief system regarding human mortality, and that they had an understanding of the use of the jars as symbolic representations of humans or as vessels for the journey to the afterlife.

title: San Diego Shipwreck Artifacts
creator: Spanish colonial shipbuilders and Asian/European craftsmen
description: In 1600, a Spanish galleon sank off Fortune Island in Batangas after a naval battle. The galleon was part of the Manila - Acapulco trade route that linked Asia and America during Spain's colonial period. A number of artifacts have been retrieved from this wreck such as cannons, porcelain, coins, weapons, and navigational instruments. This treasure trove of artifacts illustrates how extremely wealthy and globally well-connected the Philippines were during the colonial trade era and provide nonpareil examples of early maritime technologies and underwater archaeology within the area.

title: Santo Niño de Cebu Image
creator: Spanish religious sculptors
description: The Santo Niño de Cebu is a religiously significant image of the infant Jesus Christ given to Queen Juana of Cebu during Ferdinand Magellan's exploration of the Philippines in 1521. It is regarded as the oldest Christian artefact in the Philippines, and is located at the Basilica del Santo Niño in Cebu City, Philippines. Over the years, the Santo Niño has gained extraordinary importance as an embodiment of Catholicism in the Philippines. Millions of devout followers honour the Santo Niño each year, particularly during the Sinulog Festival, which is both a religious experience as well as a cultural event.

title: Homo luzonensis, also know as Callao Man Remains
creator: Early Homo species
description: This extinct species of human was found in the Cave of Callao in Cagayan Provice, on the northern part of the island of Luzon located in the region of Southeast Asia. These found fossil remains consist of teeth, bones of fingers and toes and amount to evidence that suggests that a small but distinctly different type of human lived tens of thousands of years ago. The discovery of the Homo luzonensis, dated from 2019, has changed scientists' knowledge of the earliest human migration into Southeast Asia and indicates that there may have been a number of different species of humans in the Philippines at that time. This suggests that the Philippines is an important area for studying the evolution of the human lineage.

title: Palawan Jade Artifacts
creator: Neolithic Filipino jade artisans
description:
The Palawan Jade Artifacts are ancient objects made primarily from nephrite jade that have been found in places such as the Tabon Caves. These artifacts consist of various types of ornamental jewelry, such as the well-known “lingling-o” earring, beads, bracelets, and polished stone tools.

These artifacts belong to the Neolithic period (around 2000–1500 BCE) and reveal that early Filipinos were connected to an extensive maritime trade network linking Taiwan and Southeast Asia. The level of skill in crafting these jade artifacts indicates a highly advanced ability to work with stone, as well as the status associated with jade as an expensive unique stone. According to the artifacts and the craftspeople who created them, jade was a material that conferred social distinction and was used for ornamental purposes.

title: Calatagan Burial Sites Artifacts
creator: Pre-colonial Tagalog communities
description:
The Calatagan Burial Sites in the province of Batangas are considered significant archaeological sites because they contain greater than 1000 pre-colonial graves. These graves are dated between the 14th and 15th centuries CE, and the artifacts found in them show the presence of both local earthenware and imported ceramics from China, Thailand, and Vietnam within this time period.

Artifacts that have been found in these graves include burial jars, plates, and ceramic vessels utilized for trade purposes; these artifacts indicate that early Filipinos were participants in regional maritime trade networks. These artifacts also indicate how individuals' beliefs about the afterlife and their position in society were expressed through the burial goods being deposited with their remains.
subject: Burial Practices; Ancient Tagalog Culture; Archaeology; Funerary Objects

title: Boxer Codex Illustrations
creator: Unknown Chinese/Spanish illustrators under Spanish commission
description:
The Boxer Codex contains some of the oldest European drawings of Filipinos and other Asian people from the late 16th century. It also depicts pre-colonial Filipino clothing, social class, jewelry, and custom in great detail.

These images serve as an important source of visual documentation for how Filipinos lived and interacted with each other before the arrival of the Spanish and the early years of contact with the Spaniards. They also demonstrate how different social rankings, warfare practices, and cultural identities existed within various groups in the Philippines.

title: Las Piñas Bamboo Organ
creator: Fr. Diego Cera (Spanish priest)
description:
The Las Piñas Bamboo Organ is an exceptional church instrument made primarily out of bamboo pipe built during the 19th century and completed in 1824 under the direction of Father Diego Cera and located at St. Joseph Parish Church in Las Piñas.

It is widely regarded as one of the very few examples of a predominantly bamboo organ and has a unique gentle tone created by the use of bamboo. Even though it has suffered damage from earthquakes and typhoons, it has been restored and is considered a National Cultural Treasure and a representative of Filipino music.

title: Santa Ana Site Artifacts
creator: Pre-colonial Tagalog communities (ancient inhabitants of Santa Ana, Manila)
description: Santa Ana in Manila is one of the most important pre-colonial archeological burial sites in the Philippines. The excavations have revealed more than 1,000 pieces of Chinese porcelain along with locally made pottery, beads, and other burial goods. The artifacts are dated to the Song dynasty period, indicating that Santa Ana was part of a long-established trading relationship with China. The burial materials also indicate a social hierarchy; more valuable, imported objects were often located in graves of higher status.

creator: Spanish colonial government / engineers
description: Manila's Spanish colonial district Intramuros, long since changed its role from being solely a politically, religiously, or militarily important place to being a national historical site of importance.

Fort Santiago served both as a naval fortification and as a prison for Dr. José Rizal before he was executed in 1896. As a symbol of the city's colonial past, buildings inside the walls of Fort Santiago include: the site of Fort Santiago was originally created in the late 1500s to guard the entrance of the Pasig River and protect the city of Manila against naval attacks and as historical landmarks after being restored by the Philippine government.

title: San Agustin Church
creator: Augustinian friars; Filipino laborers
description:
San Agustin Church is the Philippines' first stone church. It was built in 1607 while the Philippines was occupied by Spain. The UNESCO-listed church is an example of Baroque architecture that has been created with an earthquake-resistant design.

The building has survived through numerous earthquakes and wars over centuries and continues to be one of the most significant landmarks of religious and historical value in the country. Inside the church are intricately-carved ceilings, extensive decorations of religious art, and an extensive collection of artifacts from Spain's Colonial period.

title: Corregidor Island
creator: Spanish then American military engineers
description:
Corregidor Island sits at the mouth of Manila Bay. It was crucial to the war efforts of the US and Philippine militaries during World War II and was used as a stronghold against the Japanese.

Corregidor Island contains many war remnants including barracks, the Malinta Tunnel, and other artillery batteries. The island is now a memorial for those who served in the war, making it a very popular history site.

title: Fort Drum
creator: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
description:
Fort Drum was constructed by the United States at the beginning of the 20th Century on El Fraile Island located in Manila Bay, and it is a heavily fortified concrete structure. Fort Drum was designed as a colossal, stone battleship with heavy reinforced concrete walls and large naval guns that made it nearly indestructible.

Fort Drum served as a defensive position during WW II, however, it was eventually overrun and damaged by Japanese forces. Today it is a ship-like ruin that serves as an important historical monument related to coastal defense in the early 20th Century.

title: Cagsawa Ruins
creator: Franciscan missionaries
description:
The Cagsawa Ruins are all that remains of a 16th Century Franciscan Church that was buried by the Mayon Volcano eruption in 1814. Today the only visible structure is the bell tower, which sits partially buried under volcanic mud and ashes.

It is one of most recognizable disaster sites in the Philippines as a testament to the might of nature and also the courage and perseverance exhibited by the local populace when they rebuilt their community. The site is now a popular destination for tourists who are taking in the scenic views of Mayon Volcano.

title: Paoay Church
creator: Augustinian friars; Ilocano builders
description:
The Paoay Church, or San Agustin Church, located in the municipality of the same name, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site that features a style known as Earthquake Baroque. The church was completed in the latter part of the 17th century and uses large buttresses placed along the sides to help withstand earthquakes.

The church's coral stone and brick construction shows the influence from the Spanish colonial period while being designed to make full use of the available local building materials. Today, it is considered one of the most well-known religious buildings in Northern Philippines.

title: Vigan Historic City
creator: Spanish colonial planners; Filipino artisans
description: Vigan is another example of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognized for its preservation of Spanish Colonial architecture and lifestyle. The city also features cobblestone streets, many ancestral homes, and has an overall atmosphere of a Spanish Colonial lifestyle from the late 1600s to early 1700s. When walking along Calle Crisologo, it is like taking a trip back in time to the 18th and 19th centuries. The city of Vigan is a true blending of different cultures (Filipino, Chinese, and Spanish) and how each has influenced the course of history.

title: Barasoain Church
creator: Augustinian friars
description: Barasoain Church is considered one of the most significant historical churches in the Philippines. It has been referred to as the “Cradle of Democracy in the East” as it hosted the First Philippine Republic in 1899. During the Philippine Revolution against Spain and the early creation of the Philippines’ government, Barasoain Church was crucial. In current times, Barasoain Church continues to be a symbol of independence and democracy; it is also thought to represent national identity and unite people in these values.

title: Miagao Church
creator: Augustinian friars, local artisans
description: The Church of Santo Tomas de Villanueva was built in 1787 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The architectural style of Miagao Church is referred to as "Earthquake Baroque," and the exterior decoration features intricate carvings of local vegetation, including coconut and papaya trees, which create an interesting fusion of native Filipino and Spanish missionary aesthetics. In addition to serving as a place of worship during the Spanish colonial period, Miagao Church also functioned as a fortress to help defend against pirate raids due to its solid construction and extensive fortifications.

title: Rizal Shrine in Dapitan
creator: José Rizal (designed and built with locals)
description: The Rizal Shrine in Dapitan, Mindanao, is a restored house belonging to national hero Dr. Jose Rizal during his period of exile from 1892 until he was executed on December 30, 1896. During his time in Dapitan, Rizal practiced medicine, educated local children, conducted scientific research and developed projects to improve the communities where he lived. The shrine contains his residence, clinic, school and farming areas, all demonstrating his incredible range of talents and contributions to society during the period of his exile and today serves as a museum that honors his life and accomplishments.

title: Aguinaldo Shrine
creator: Emilio Aguinaldo (designed/modified residence)
description:
Emilio Aguinaldo’s family home serves as the Aguinaldo Shrine, where Aguinaldo was the first President of the Philippines. It is here that the Philippines declared independence from Spain on June 12, 1898.

The house has a beautiful balcony where they first raised the Philippine flag and played the National Anthem. It now operates as a museum containing revolutionary artifacts and historical documents.

title: Leyte Landing Memorial
creator: American government / WWII memorial designers
description:
The Leyte Landing Memorial, also known as the MacArthur Landing Memorial, commemorates the return of General Douglas MacArthur to the Philippines on October 20, 1944 during World War II. This event marked the beginning of the liberation of the country from Japanese occupation.

The site features large bronze statues of MacArthur and his troops wading ashore in Leyte Gulf, symbolizing the fulfillment of his famous promise, “I shall return.”

title: Baluarte de San Diego
creator: Spanish military engineers
description:
In Intramuros, one of the oldest stone forts that were built by the Spaniards in the last part of the 1500's, is called the Baluarte de San Diego (Baluarte = Fort). This fort was built as a circular fortification to defend the city of Manila from attack (i.e., to create a protective barrier around) from foreign countries. 

Since it has been destroyed and rebuilt many times throughout its history, especially in times of war and earthquakes, the Baluarte de San Diego has become a historical site with beautiful gardens and remnants of the Spanish military architectural style.

title: Banaue Rice Terraces
creator: Ifugao ancestors (indigenous farmers)
description:
The Banaue Rice Terraces are ancient agricultural landscapes that were built by the indigenous Ifugao peoples on the mountains of Ifugao 2,000 years ago. They have been called the “Eighth Wonder of the World” due to their impressive size and precision of engineering.

The terraces have a complex irrigation system that moves water from the forests above them into the terraces for rice farming on the steep mountain slopes. They represent great indigenous knowledge and sustainability, and they provide a living example of cultural heritage.

title: Tabon Cave Complex
creator: Early prehistoric Filipino communities (no single creator)
description:
The Tabon Cave Complex in Palawan is among the most ancient archaeologically significant sites in the Philippines, and it is referred to as the “Father of Philippines Civilization," since it contains the two oldest human remains found in the Philippines, namely, the Tabon Man fossil.

The excavations have yielded evidence of human activity dating back tens of thousands of years in the form of stone tools, pottery, and burials. The caves demonstrate that the first humans to live in the Philippines were there long before there were written records of their existence.

title: Magellan's Cross
creator: Spanish and Portuguese explorers (Ferdinand Magellan expedition)
description:
In 1521 after reaching Cebu, the Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan erected Magellan's Cross, a wooden Christian cross. This event represented the beginning of the introduction of Christianity to the Philippines.

It is thought that the original cross lies enclosed in another cross made of wood for protection. The place exists within a small chapel near the Basilica del Santo Niño and continues to represent an important religious and historical event.

title: Taal Basilica
creator: Augustinian friars; Filipino craftsmen
description:
Taal Basilica (also known as: Basilica de San Martin de Tours) is one of the largest Roman Catholic churches in Asia; it was built during the Spanish colonization of the Philippines. It is an excellent example of Earthquake Baroque architecture, built to be resistant to earthquakes.

The church has been rebuilt various times as a result of the eruption of the volcanoes and earthquakes but continues to serve as a major religious and community center in Batangas.

title: Daraga Church
creator: Franciscan friars; Bicolano laborers
description: Officially called Nuestra Señora de la Porteria Parish Church, the Daraga Church is made from baroque-style and completed in 1773 by Franciscan Missionaries. Known for having a thick volcanic stone footings and a highly decorative exterior finish, the Daraga Church provides a great view of Mayon Volcano. It represents one of the best examples of Earthquake Baroque architecture, and has stood up to numerous volcanic eruptions and other natural disasters making it both a religious symbol and an important part of our history and culture.

title: Pinaglabanan Shrine
creator: Philippine Revolutionary forces; National Historical Commission of the Philippines (commemorative site builders)
description:
The Battle of San Juan del Monte in 1896 was one of the first major battles in the Philippine Revolution against Spanish colonization, and the Pinaglabanan Shrine was built to honor this battle. On August 30, 1896, members within the revolutionary group, the Katipunan, attempted to seize a Spanish munitions depot at San Juan del Monte; they lost the battle, yet this battle sparked a wave of rebellion against Spanish rule.

Today, the Pinaglabanan Shrine includes a museum and memorial park that pay tribute to the valour of early Filipino revolutionaries.

title: Sandugo Shrine
creator: Boholano people (historical event commemorated); National Historical Commission of the Philippines (monument designers)
description:
The Sandugo Shrine commemorates the Blood Compact (or Sandugo) established between Spanish explorer Miguel López de Legazpi and Datu Sikatuna, a local Bohol chief, in 1565. The Blood Compact was regarded as a demonstration of friendship and alliance between the Spanish and Filipinos.

The Sandugo Shrine has several sculptures depicting the ceremonial blood compact, which serve as a reminder of the early diplomatic relationships between Spain and the Philippines.

title: San Sebastian Church
creator: Spanish engineers (Genaro Palacios design)
description:
The Basilica Minore de San Sebastian, or San Sebastián Church, is a unique example of a Gothic Revival style of architecture located in Manila, and it is the only all-steel church in Asia. It was prefabricated in Belgium in the 19th century, and upon completion was assembled together in the Philippines in 1891.

The architecture of San Sebastián Church was engineered in such a way as to withstand earthquakes, as well as having beautiful stained-glass windows and other elaborate examples of Gothic Architecture on the inside. It is said to be one of the most architecturally unique churches found in the country.

title: Casa Manila
creator: Imelda Marcos (conceptualization); Filipino heritage architects and craftsmen
description:
Casa Manila is a reconstructed Spanish Colonial-style house located in Intramuros and was built to imitate how wealthy Filipino families lived in the late 19th century when the Spanish Colonizers ruled over the Philippines.

At the Casa Manila Museum, one will find a variety of antiques that are representative of the decorations and materials that were popular during the Spanish Colonial era, as well as examples of furniture and elaborate wrought-iron railings that were typical of the period.

title: Fort Pilar
creator: Spanish military engineers
description: Zamboanga City is home to Fort Pilar, a 17th century Spanish fortress that served as protection against pirates and foreign countries. In present-day Zamboanga City, Fort Pillar is a significant historical reference point while also serving as a place of worship to Our Lady of the Pillar. As such, the site remains one of Mindanao's most important cultural and spiritual places.

title: The Ruins (Negros Occidental)
creator: Don Mariano Ledesma Lacson (commissioned mansion builders)
description: The Ruins are the remnants of a magnificent mansion built in the early 1900s by sugar baron Don Mariano Ledesma Lacson in Negros Occidental, Philippines. The ruins were torched during World War II to stop the Japanese military from using the mansion as a base of operations; today they consist of beautiful and expansive pieces of concrete columns and other structures that have outlived their original mode but still exhibit their former splendor. Because of the romantic and tragic story of this mansion, some people refer to it as the “Taj Mahal of Negros.”
